analysis: After the Skeptic's review - the lazy-representation method L(n) = Psi(lazy(n)) + (second phase) agrees with full simulation of the strategy game for every n < 20,000; the conjectured recursion CLM-C19-05 agrees with it on all 103,799 tested n (all n < 10^5, 3000 random n < 10^15, 800 numbers F_j + m with j = 30..69); the second phase has at most B(n) - Psi(lazy(n)) <= 1 + (t+1)(t+6)/2 moves on every tested n (largest ratio to the bound 0.476); 26, 53, 81 and 109 second-phase moves at n = 10^6, 10^9, 10^15, 10^18.
assumptions: the strategy game is optimal (Cusenza et al. 2022, Thm 1.2) - needed only to call its length L(n); the identity with the simulated strategy game is unconditional
random samples with a fixed seed
falsification: Any mismatch with full simulation (would contradict Theorems 1-2), any violated bound, or any n where the recursion and the method disagree (would refute CLM-C19-05).

methodology: Compare with greedy_length_fast for every n < 20000; compare longest_rec (the recursion) with the method for every n < 100000, 3000 random n in [1e6, 1e15) and 800 n = F_j + m (j = 30..69, m < F_(j-1)); check second-phase moves <= B(n) - Psi(lazy(n)) <= 1 + (t + 1)(t + 6)/2 on all tested n; time the method, the recursion and (n <= 1e7) full simulation.
question: Does L(n) = Psi(lazy(n)) + (second phase from lazy(n)) agree with full simulation, does the move bound hold, and does the conjectured recursion agree with this provably correct method on far more n than before?
